breakthroughs.title: Meta FAIR ESMFold Maps 617 Million+ Metagenomic Protein Structures 60× Faster via 15B Language Model
breakthroughs.aiSystem: ESMFold (15B-Parameter ESM-2 Protein Language Model, Meta FAIR)
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Published in Science, Meta’s 15B-parameter ESMFold proved protein language models predict atomic 3D structures directly from single sequences 60× faster—folding 617M+ (later 772M) dark-proteome proteins in two weeks.
breakthroughs.summary: Published in Science on March 17, 2023 (following a November 2022 atlas release), Zeming Lin, Alexander Rives, and the Meta FAIR Protein Team demonstrated that scaling masked protein language models (ESM-2) to 15 billion parameters causes atomic-resolution 3D structural information to emerge directly inside sequence representations. Pairing ESM-2 with an equivariant folding head created ESMFold, which predicts atomic protein structures directly from a single sequence without slow multiple-sequence alignments (MSAs)—achieving up to 60× faster inference than AlphaFold 2. Released the open-access ESM Metagenomic Atlas, illuminating millions of "dark proteome" sequences with no known homologs.
breakthroughs.caveats: Slightly lower atomic accuracy than AlphaFold 2 on proteins where deep multiple-sequence alignments are available, though uniquely advantaged on orphan and metagenomic sequences.

breakthroughs.title: AlphaTensor: Reinforcement Learning Discovers Faster Matrix Multiplication

Discovered >14,000 non-equivalent rank-49 4×4 factorizations, revealing unexpected richness in algebraic complexity.
Pioneered the autonomous algorithm-discovery lineage culminating in FunSearch (2023) and AlphaEvolve (2025).
breakthroughs.caveats: The 47-multiplication 4×4 breakthrough held in finite-field (characteristic 2) arithmetic rather than real/complex numbers—a gap later closed by AlphaEvolve's 48-multiplication complex algorithm in 2025.

breakthroughs.title: FermiNet Solves the Many-Electron Schrödinger Equation from First Principles
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: First deep-learning wavefunction ansatz to solve the many-electron Schrödinger equation from first principles at chemical accuracy—without external training data—outperforming coupled cluster on stretched bonds.
breakthroughs.summary: Published in Physical Review Research in September 2020 by David Pfau, James Spencer, Alexander Matthews, and W. M. C. Foulkes (DeepMind & Imperial College London), FermiNet introduced a permutation-equivariant neural network architecture obeying the Pauli exclusion principle by construction. Trained purely via variational energy minimization on physics alone (zero external training datasets), FermiNet achieved chemical accuracy across atoms, small molecules, and strongly correlated stretched bonds where gold-standard CCSD(T) breaks down, launching neural quantum Monte Carlo for chemistry and condensed-matter physics.
technicalHighlights: Replaces fixed single-electron orbitals inside Slater determinants with many-electron neural orbitals, capturing rich electron correlation while strictly preserving fermionic antisymmetry.
Requires no precomputed quantum-chemistry training dataset—optimizing the wavefunction directly against the physical Hamiltonian via variational quantum Monte Carlo.
Outperformed gold-standard coupled-cluster CCSD(T) on bond dissociation and strongly correlated chains (such as H₁₀) and later uncovered Fermi-liquid-to-Wigner-crystal transitions in electron gases.
breakthroughs.caveats: High computational scaling (roughly O(N⁴) in electron count) limits ab initio FermiNet calculations to molecules and unit cells with tens of electrons rather than large biomolecules.

scoreRationale.foundational: Established neural wavefunctions as a first-principles ab initio method competitive with and surpassing classical quantum chemistry benchmarks.
scoreRationale.ripple: Catalyzed an entire subfield of neural quantum Monte Carlo (Psiformer, PauliNet, periodic FermiNet) spanning chemistry and condensed-matter physics.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed in Physical Review Research (2, 033429), open-sourced, and independently reproduced across dozens of follow-up papers.
scoreRationale.velocity: Achieved breakthrough variational accuracy directly from the Schrödinger equation, though compute costs remain substantial.

breakthroughs.title: Complete Resolution of Keller’s 1930 Cube-Tiling Conjecture in Dimension 7 via Machine-Verified SAT Proof
breakthroughs.aiSystem: CaDiCaL SAT Solver + Formally Verified DRAT / Symmetry-Breaking Proof
breakthroughs.aiTimeToSolve: CPU-hours on cluster (20 GB DRAT proof)
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Completely settled Otto-Heinrich Keller’s 90-year-old geometry conjecture (1930) in its final open dimension (d = 7), proving via a formally certified SAT proof that every 7D unit-cube tiling contains a face-sharing pair.
breakthroughs.summary: In July 2020 (IJCAR 2020, later published in Journal of the ACM), Joshua Brakensiek, Marijn J. H. Heule, John Mackey, and David Narváez completely resolved Otto-Heinrich Keller’s 1930 conjecture on space-filling unit cube tilings. Prior mathematicians had proven the conjecture true for dimensions d ≤ 6 (Perron, 1940) and false for d ≥ 8 (Lagarias & Shor, 1992; Mackey, 2002), leaving dimension 7 as the sole open case for decades. Encoding the non-existence of a size-128 clique in the Keller graphs G_{7,3}, G_{7,4}, and G_{7,6} into propositional logic with automated symmetry breaking, the CaDiCaL SAT solver proved unsatisfiability and emitted an optimized ~20 GB clausal proof certified by formally verified DRAT proof checkers.
technicalHighlights: Settled the last remaining open dimension (d = 7) of Keller’s 1930 conjecture, completing a 90-year classification across all dimensions.
Combined propositional symmetry breaking with CaDiCaL SAT solving to rule out size-128 cliques in the Keller graphs.
Produced a compact ~20 GB clausal unsatisfiability certificate validated by formally verified proof checkers (ACL2/Coq/Isabelle ecosystem).
breakthroughs.caveats: The propositional encoding reduction relies on established graph-theoretic reductions by Corrádi–Szabó and Kisielewicz, while the exhaustive search and clausal symmetry breaking are machine-checked.

scoreRationale.foundational: Completely closed a famous 90-year-old problem in discrete geometry generalizing Minkowski’s 1907 lattice-tiling theorem.
scoreRationale.ripple: Cemented automated SAT solving + verified clausal proofs as a mainstream instrument for settling intractable combinatorial geometry problems.
scoreRationale.verification: Formally certified via DRAT proof checking and peer-reviewed in IJCAR 2020 and Journal of the ACM.
scoreRationale.velocity: Resolved a search space far beyond human casework via automated symmetry breaking and parallel SAT solving.

breakthroughs.summary: Published in Nature on March 28, 2018, Marwin H. S. Segler, Mike Preuss, and Mark P. Waller at the University of Münster broke a 60-year bottleneck in computer-aided organic synthesis planning (dating back to E. J. Corey’s pioneering 1960s LHASA program). Trained on roughly 12 million published organic reactions, their 3N-MCTS neuro-symbolic system combined Monte Carlo Tree Search with three neural networks (an expansion policy, an in-scope reaction filter, and a rollout policy) to plan multi-step retrosynthetic routes autonomously. It solved nearly twice as many target molecules 30× faster than classical heuristic tools, and in a double-blind A/B evaluation, expert organic chemists judged its computer-generated routes equivalent in quality to published human literature syntheses.
technicalHighlights: Trained three deep neural networks on ~12 million published organic reactions and coupled them to symbolic Monte Carlo Tree Search (3N-MCTS).
Solved ~2× more organic target molecules 30× faster than classical rule-based retrosynthesis engines.
First automated synthesis planner whose routes were indistinguishable from human literature routes in a double-blind chemist evaluation.
breakthroughs.caveats: Evaluated via double-blind route quality and benchmark solve rates rather than robotic wet-lab synthesis of every proposed route; stereochemistry and rare reaction conditions remained active follow-up challenges.

scoreRationale.foundational: Landmark neuro-symbolic breakthrough in chemistry—translating AlphaGo-style MCTS + neural policies to solve a 60-year grand challenge in organic retrosynthesis.
scoreRationale.ripple: Became the foundational paradigm for modern automated synthesis planning (AiZynthFinder, ASKCOS, Coscientist, robotic synthesis labs).
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed in Nature (Vol. 555, pp. 604–610) with double-blind expert chemist evaluation.
scoreRationale.velocity: Delivered a 30× speedup over legacy computer-aided synthesis tools while doubling solvability.

breakthroughs.title: Google Brain & NASA Deep Neural Network Discovers Exoplanet Kepler-90i, First Known 8-Planet Analog System
breakthroughs.aiSystem: AstroNet (Deep Convolutional Neural Network, Google Brain / NASA)
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: A deep CNN trained on 15,000 Kepler light curves discovered two missed exoplanets—including Kepler-90i, making Kepler-90 the first known star system tying our Solar System’s eight confirmed planets.
breakthroughs.summary: Announced by NASA on December 14, 2017 and published in The Astronomical Journal (2018), Google Brain engineer Christopher J. Shallue and NASA Sagan Fellow Andrew Vanderburg built AstroNet, a deep convolutional neural network trained on 15,000 labeled Kepler transit signals to distinguish true planetary transits from astrophysical false positives. Scanning 670 previously searched multi-planet stars, the neural network detected weak periodic transit signals missed by all prior human and classical automated pipelines—discovering Kepler-80g (completing a 5-planet resonant chain) and Kepler-90i, a rocky super-Earth that made Kepler-90 the first confirmed eight-planet exoplanet system matching our Solar System.
technicalHighlights: Trained a deep CNN (AstroNet) on global and local folded Kepler photometric light curves with ~96% classification accuracy.
Discovered two confirmed exoplanets (Kepler-90i and Kepler-80g) hidden in faint transit signals overlooked by all previous pipelines.
Established Kepler-90 as the first confirmed 8-planet system outside our Solar System and open-sourced AstroNet for TESS/K2 surveys.
breakthroughs.caveats: Neural-network detections still required follow-up statistical validation by human astronomers to rule out background eclipsing binaries and instrumental artifacts.

scoreRationale.foundational: First high-profile discovery of new confirmed worlds by a deep neural network mining archival telescope telemetry.
scoreRationale.ripple: Popularized deep-learning vetting pipelines across NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS exoplanet surveys and broader time-domain astronomy.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed in The Astronomical Journal (doi:10.3847/1538-3881/aa9e09) and officially confirmed by NASA.
scoreRationale.velocity: Automatically uncovered faint multi-planet signals across hundreds of archival star systems missed over years of prior searches.

breakthroughs.title: Schur Number Five (S(5) = 160) Settled After 101 Years via Formally Certified 2-Petabyte SAT Proof
breakthroughs.aiSystem: Cube-and-Conquer SAT Solver (Massively Parallel SAT + Certified DRAT Checker)
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Marijn Heule settled Issai Schur’s 101-year-old Ramsey-theory problem (1916), proving S(5) = 160 via massively parallel SAT solving and certifying a record 2-petabyte proof with a formally verified checker.
breakthroughs.summary: Posted on November 21, 2017 (and published at AAAI-18), Marijn J. H. Heule at the University of Texas at Austin resolved the century-old Schur Number Five problem posed by Issai Schur in 1916: finding the largest integer n such that {1, …, n} can be 5-colored without a monochromatic solution to a + b = c. Encoding the problem into propositional logic and applying massively parallel Cube-and-Conquer SAT solving on the Stampede supercomputer, Heule proved S(5) = 160 and validated the resulting 2-petabyte unsatisfiability proof—ten times larger than the 2016 Pythagorean Triples proof—using a formally verified proof checker.
technicalHighlights: Settled Issai Schur’s 1916 Ramsey-theory problem after 101 years, proving S(5) = 160.
Constructed and mechanically certified a 2-petabyte clausal proof—demonstrating formal verification scales to petabyte-class automated reasoning.
Advanced Cube-and-Conquer partitioning heuristics subsequently used to resolve Keller’s Conjecture in dimension 7.
breakthroughs.caveats: The 2-petabyte proof is purely machine-verifiable rather than human-readable, offering no short conceptual explanation for why 160 is the exact threshold.

scoreRationale.foundational: Resolved a classical 101-year-old problem in Ramsey theory and additive combinatorics.
scoreRationale.ripple: Proved that formally verified SAT proof checkers can scale to petabyte-level automated mathematical proofs.
scoreRationale.verification: Certified end-to-end by a formally verified clausal proof checker and peer-reviewed at AAAI-18.
scoreRationale.velocity: Cracked a combinatorial coloring threshold that resisted a century of mathematical and computational attacks.

breakthroughs.title: Boolean Pythagorean Triples Problem Solved via Cube-and-Conquer SAT
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Pioneering pre-neural symbolic AI milestone: resolved a 30-year Ramsey theory problem via a 200-terabyte machine-verified SAT proof.
breakthroughs.summary: Marijn Heule, Oliver Kullmann, and Victor Marek encoded Ronald Graham’s longstanding Boolean Pythagorean Triples problem—whether the positive integers can be 2-colored with no monochromatic solution to a² + b² = c²—into propositional logic and solved it via Cube-and-Conquer SAT search. The solver proved 1..7,824 is 2-colorable while 1..7,825 is impossible, producing a 200 TB DRAT proof certificate later formally verified in Coq.
technicalHighlights: Partitioned the search space into one million sub-problems (“cubes”) solved in two days across 800 cores on the Stampede supercomputer.
Established the exact threshold at n = 7,825—the largest mathematical proof certificate generated up to that time (200 TB uncompressed, 68 GB compressed).
Independently verified by formal checkers extracted from Coq, proving symbolic search could settle open combinatorial problems beyond human casework.
breakthroughs.caveats: A pure classical SAT/symbolic search milestone rather than deep learning; while 100% machine-verified, the 200 TB proof offers little human-readable structural intuition and required bespoke symmetry breaking.

scoreRationale.foundational: Settled a famous open Ramsey theory conjecture posed by Ronald Graham and established the exact critical coloring threshold.
scoreRationale.ripple: Demonstrated scalable machine-checked proof certificates (DRAT) and directly foreshadowed hybrid formal-verification pipelines.
scoreRationale.verification: Machine-checked via DRAT certificates and independently verified in Coq—gold-standard formal certainty.
scoreRationale.velocity: Solved a 30-year open problem in two days of parallel symbolic search, yet remained restricted to finite combinatorial encodings.

breakthroughs.title: Robot Scientist “Adam” Autonomously Discovers New Yeast Gene Functions
breakthroughs.aiSystem: Robot Scientist Adam (Abductive Logic + Lab Robotics)
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Historic pre-neural benchmark: the first closed-loop autonomous AI system to formulate hypotheses, run physical lab experiments, and publish new biological knowledge.
breakthroughs.summary: Developed by Ross King and colleagues at Aberystwyth and Cambridge, Robot Scientist “Adam” combined symbolic abductive logic programming, formal biological ontologies, and automated wet-lab robotics to investigate orphan enzymes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Without human intervention in the loop, Adam formulated 20 hypotheses identifying genes encoding orphan enzymes, designed and executed growth assays, confirmed 12 hypotheses, and had its key discoveries independently validated by manual human biochemistry.
technicalHighlights: First physical machine to execute the full scientific method autonomously—hypothesis generation, experiment design, wet-lab execution, and result interpretation.
Identified three previously unannotated yeast genes encoding the orphan enzyme 2-aminoadipate transaminase (confirmed manually via wet-lab enzyme assays).
Demonstrated end-to-end formalization of experimental metadata and reasoning decades before LLM-based AI Co-Scientists.
breakthroughs.caveats: Relied on rigid symbolic logic rules and domain-specific yeast ontologies; it could not generalize outside narrowly encoded metabolic models—highlighting why modern neural foundation models triggered a phase transition.

scoreRationale.foundational: Proved in principle that an autonomous AI system can independently discover genuine new empirical scientific knowledge.
scoreRationale.ripple: Inspired the entire self-driving laboratory and autonomous AI scientist movement, culminating in systems like Google AI Co-Scientist.
scoreRationale.verification: Published in Science with human wet-lab biochemical verification of Adam’s newly discovered gene–enzyme mappings.
scoreRationale.velocity: Pioneered automated experimental cycles, though narrow symbolic engineering kept throughput modest compared to 2025–2026 foundation models.

breakthroughs.title: Automated Theorem Prover EQP Solves the 63-Year-Old Robbins Conjecture
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: The foundational pre-neural milestone in autonomous AI mathematics: solved a 63-year-old algebra conjecture that defeated Alfred Tarski.
breakthroughs.summary: Posed by Herbert Robbins in 1933 and studied unsuccessfully by Alfred Tarski and generations of algebraists, the Robbins Conjecture asked whether every Robbins algebra is a Boolean algebra. On October 10, 1996, William McCune’s specialized symbolic equational prover EQP at Argonne National Laboratory autonomously discovered a complete proof in eight days on a workstation, outputting a machine-checked proof object later simplified and formalized in Isabelle/HOL.
technicalHighlights: Used associative-commutative (AC) unification and paramodulation strategies in EQP to prove Winker’s sufficient condition automatically.
First widely celebrated resolution of a longstanding open mathematical conjecture by a fully autonomous computer reasoning program.
Produced a complete machine-verifiable proof object checked independently, later streamlined by Dahn (1998) and formalized in the Archive of Formal Proofs.
breakthroughs.caveats: Required extensive human algebraic reductions (Winker’s lemmas) and hand-crafted equational search heuristics; pure symbolic provers remained largely isolated to narrow algebraic/logic niches for the next two decades until neural networks arrived.

scoreRationale.foundational: Resolved a famous 63-year-old foundational algebra problem that resisted Alfred Tarski and decades of human mathematicians.
scoreRationale.ripple: Became the canonical proof-of-concept for automated mathematical discovery, directly motivating generations of ATP and formal verification research.
scoreRationale.verification: Produced a machine-checked formal proof object verified by independent checkers and published in the Journal of Automated Reasoning.
scoreRationale.velocity: Closed a 63-year open problem in 8 days of workstation search—though symbolic provers only achieved a handful of such wins across the next 24 years.

breakthroughs.title: Graffiti Autonomously Generates Novel Graph Theory Conjectures Studied by Erdős & Chung
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: First automated mathematical conjecturing system to produce genuinely novel open conjectures that sparked ~80 peer-reviewed papers by leading mathematicians.
breakthroughs.summary: Developed by Siemion Fajtlowicz at the University of Houston and publicly unveiled in 1986 with its first 18 conjectures, Graffiti searched algebraic expressions across graph invariants and retained candidate inequalities holding without counterexample across a curated graph database—later refined with the Dalmatian informativeness heuristic. Its conjectures in graph theory and mathematical chemistry (fullerenes) proved deep enough to inspire roughly 80 published papers by mathematicians including Paul Erdős, Fan Chung, Béla Bollobás, Noga Alon, and László Lovász.
technicalHighlights: Autonomously generated Graffiti Conjecture 2 (average distance ≤ independence number for any connected graph), proved by Fan Chung in 1988, and the residue–independence inequality proved by Favaron, Mahéo, and Saclé in 1991.
Introduced the Dalmatian heuristic to suppress true-but-trivial statements by retaining only inequalities strictly sharper than all prior bounds on at least one graph.
Extended into mathematical chemistry, formulating novel structural conjectures on fullerene and benzenoid molecular graphs.
breakthroughs.caveats: Generated conjectures empirically from finite graph databases rather than proving theorems; many candidate inequalities were later refuted by counterexamples, illustrating both the power and fragility of pure symbolic heuristic search.

scoreRationale.foundational: Demonstrated empirically that a computer program can originate genuinely novel, non-trivial mathematical hypotheses rather than merely checking human proofs.
scoreRationale.ripple: Sparked ~80 peer-reviewed papers across combinatorics and mathematical chemistry and established the automated conjecturing lineage leading to DeepMind Knot Theory and AlphaEvolve.
scoreRationale.verification: Multiple core Graffiti conjectures were formally proved and published in top refereed venues (Discrete Mathematics, Journal of Graph Theory) by leading mathematicians.
scoreRationale.velocity: Compressed systematic exploration of invariant inequalities across hundreds of graphs, though narrow symbolic templates limited scope to inequality-form conjectures.

breakthroughs.title: Meta-DENDRAL Discovers Novel Mass-Spectrometry Rules Published in JACS
breakthroughs.whyItMatters: Widely regarded as the earliest peer-reviewed scientific discovery made by a machine learning system—inferring new chemical fragmentation rules accepted in JACS.
breakthroughs.summary: Built at Stanford by Bruce Buchanan, Dennis Smith, Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg, and Carl Djerassi as the rule-learning companion to Heuristic DENDRAL, Meta-DENDRAL analyzed empirical mass spectra and molecular structures of aliphatic amines and ketoandrostanes to induce new bond-cleavage fragmentation rules automatically. Published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society in October 1976, several of Meta-DENDRAL’s induced rules for mono- and polyketoandrostanes were judged novel by chemists and entered the refereed chemical literature.
technicalHighlights: Used a theory-constrained generate-and-test rule-induction pipeline (RULEGEN and RULEMOD) to learn interpretable chemical cleavage rules directly from empirical spectra.
Discovered previously unformulated mass-spectrometry fragmentation rules for mono-, di-, and triketoandrostanes published in JACS (1976).
Established the knowledge-rich machine learning paradigm and directly inspired Tom Mitchell’s version-space framework and subsequent AI-for-chemistry systems.
breakthroughs.caveats: Operated inside a tightly hand-engineered symbolic chemistry representation and required substantial expert curation; its rules were domain-specific analytical heuristics rather than general physical laws.

scoreRationale.foundational: Marked the historical birth of AI-assisted scientific rule discovery by producing novel, publishable chemical rules from empirical data.
scoreRationale.ripple: Catalyzed decades of cheminformatics, expert systems, and machine learning for molecular inference—the 50-year ancestor of modern AI chemistry.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed and published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS 98(20): 6168–6178) and empirically validated against spectral data.
scoreRationale.velocity: Automated tedious spectral rule induction that previously required expert chemists, though handcrafted LISP knowledge bases limited throughput.
